text: Socrates begins his city with need. No one is self-sufficient, and so the first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each doing the one work his nature suits (Republic 369b–370c). A city that stayed at that size would never need a soldier. Glaucon refuses to live there. He wants couches and side dishes, and Socrates grants him a city with a fever (372d–e). Once appetite grows past what the healthy city required, war follows: the land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one, and the city must take its neighbors' land and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors comes of necessity, and with it the question that occupies the rest of the reading. What kind of person can be trusted with weapons? Socrates finds his model in a well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–e). From the dog he draws the first of the city's many surprises. The guardian tells friend from enemy by knowledge, and for that reason he is already a philosopher of a kind (376a–c).
